edges.description: Colonizing organisms are taken up by, and survive within, airway macrophages.
Bacterial lipopolysaccharide drives a Toll-like-receptor-4-dependent inflammatory response in the colonized airway.
After cycles of intracellular replication the organism spreads systemically and re-enters the bloodstream.
Intramacrophage infection drives the pro-inflammatory response.
Unrestrained airway inflammation contributes to tissue destruction and necrotizing pneumonia.
Systemic cytokine release contributes to septic shock.
The systemic inflammatory response produces the high fever of the acute syndrome.
The acute inflammatory response produces the accompanying leukocytosis.
The acute-phase inflammatory response raises the erythrocyte sedimentation rate.
Bloodstream infection drives the systemic septic response.
Circulating organisms are detected as positive blood cultures.
The necrotizing lesion is the clinical pneumonia.
Destruction of lung parenchyma produces progressive respiratory failure.
Lung destruction produces a rapid decline in pulmonary function.
The systemic response manifests clinically as sepsis.
Cystic fibrosis airway disease permits chronic BCC colonization, the substrate for cepacia syndrome.
Loss of the phagocyte oxidative burst permits BCC survival within phagocytes, predisposing to invasive disease.

edges.limitations: Larval zebrafish have no cystic fibrosis airway background and no mature adaptive immunity at the stage assayed, so the model reports intramacrophage replication and the lethal inflammatory response without the chronic-colonization context that precedes the human syndrome, and no single animal model reproduces the full human cepacia-syndrome triad.

nodes.description: Because the organism is intrinsically multidrug-resistant, cepacia syndrome is treated with aggressive combinations of intravenous and inhaled antimicrobials, most often including cotrimoxazole (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole), ceftazidime, a carbapenem such as meropenem, and inhaled or enteral agents such as tobramycin and minocycline.

nodes.description: Burkholderia cepacia complex is a facultative intracellular pathogen that survives and replicates within macrophages by interfering with phagosome maturation; in vivo the intramacrophage stage is required for bacterial proliferation and drives the fatal pro-inflammatory response. The intracellular niche also helps exclude poorly cell-penetrant antibiotics.

nodes.description: Burkholderia cepacia complex bacteria are constitutively resistant to many antibiotic classes through efflux pumps and their outer-membrane composition, so standard regimens frequently fail regardless of in vitro findings. This is a therapeutic-vulnerability node, not a step in the causal cascade.

nodes.description: Burkholderia cepacia complex lipopolysaccharide activates TLR4/CD14 signaling in monocytes and macrophages, driving MAP-kinase and NF-kappaB-dependent release of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF and IL-6.
